description.text:
English promotional cards that belong to no numbered expansion or Black Star Promo run, gathered here as one set. Cards like these are usually handed out with merchandise tied to recent expansions or to events elsewhere in the Pokémon franchise, through limited in-store promotions and tours, and at high-profile events. Wizards of the Coast made only a handful between 1999 and 2002, and they grew in number after Pokémon USA, now The Pokémon Company International, took over the game in 2003. Stamped and foil versions of numbered cards, which Bulbapedia counts among them, are listed with the cards they reprint rather than here.

Among them are Ancient Mew, given with a ticket to The Power of One in the first week of its run in cinemas in 2000; the No. 1 Trainer trophy cards, awarded to the champion of each age division at the World Championships since 2004, the first held under Pokémon USA; and the Victory Medals awarded at Battle Road tournaments in the United States from spring 2007 to spring 2011.

description.text:
A prototype of an English Pokémon card, made by Wizards of the Coast in mid-1998 before Base Set came out. Its text is a near-literal translation of the Japanese cards of the time: it says "Level 2" where Base Set says "Stage 2", "escape" for the retreat cost and "Special Powers" for Rain Dance, and gives Blastoise LV.52. It is numbered 009/165R and has no set or rarity symbol. The art is not Base Set's: it is Ken Sugimori's Blastoise from the Japanese Trade Please! promo, which is also the Pokémon Blue box art.

Wizards ran the card on test sheets alongside Magic: The Gathering cards, so most copies have a Magic back. CGC compared the print rosettes and found every version came from the same plates. The first copies surfaced in 2016 and were dismissed as fakes at first; CGC examined and graded them in 2020. No other Pokémon is known from these sheets.

description.text:
A card of Doug Ferguson, Senior Vice President of Product Development at The Pokémon Company International, made as a going-away gift when he left in 2019 after 16 years at the company. Mike Cressy, who drew Ishihara-GX, illustrated it, and it carries the same number, TPCi01. Collectors learned of it in June 2020, when Ferguson showed it on his own company website.

Ferguson was given five poster-sized copies, 18 by 25 inches, with blank backs that carry a press approval sticker. CGC certified four of them in October 2026; the fifth stays framed in his collection. A standard-sized copy, unknown until then, was authenticated by CGC in 2024.

description.text: A card of Tsunekazu Ishihara, president of The Pokémon Company and the man who led the creation of the Pokémon TCG, drawn by Mike Cressy as a full-art Pokémon-GX. The cards were presented to Ishihara, who handed them out himself to guests at his private party at the Country Music Hall of Fame on 26 August 2018, during the World Championships in Nashville. How many exist is unknown; by July 2023 CGC had graded twelve, one of them signed by Ishihara with a small Pikachu sketch.

description.text: The English jumbo for the GameCube game Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness, whose logo sits in the corner of its picture; in Japan the card came with Pokémon Scoop at Pokémon Festa 2005. It was first handed out, unannounced, at the game's US launch party at the Nintendo World Store in New York on 2 October 2005, the day before the game went on sale, to fans who queued to play it. Later that month it was given away at IGN Live in Anaheim and at the Electronic Game Show in Mexico City, and a smaller batch went out at a Pokémon 10th anniversary event at Space Center Houston on 25 March 2006. Shadow Lugia has 300 HP and one attack, Shadow Storm, for 1,000 damage. Collectors warn that fakes are common.
